request.system:
You write one blog article for an online shop from a plan. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, and the plan.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

Title: How to Make Cold Brew Coffee at Home: Ratio, Grind and Steep Time
Angle: The reader will learn what cold brew is, the coffee-to-water ratio, grind size and steep time that work, a step-by-step method in a dedicated jar or a French press, and how to choose beans and serve the concentrate.
## What cold brew is, and why time replaces heat
   Cold brew is an immersion method: coarse coffee steeps in cold water for many hours instead of minutes in hot water. This gives a smooth, low-bitterness concentrate. It also explains how cold brew differs from iced coffee. (F2, F10)
## What you need
   Equipment checklist: a vessel with a filter, a burr grinder that can grind coarse, a scale, cold filtered water and fresh beans. Introduces the Cold Brew Jar as the dedicated option. (F1, F3, F4, F5, F8)
## Ratio and grind size
   A starting concentrate ratio of about 1:10 coffee to water (150 g to 1.5 litres), and why a coarse, French-press-level grind matters. Fines make the brew muddy and over-extracted. The Hand Grinder covers this coarse range, but its hopper holds 25 g, so 150 g means grinding in about six loads. For larger batches, browse the grinder collection. (F6, F7, F26, F27, F28, F25)
## Step by step: making cold brew in the jar
   1. Weigh and grind the coffee. 2. Fill the filter basket. 3. Pour cold water slowly to wet all the grounds. 4. Seal the jar and refrigerate. 5. Steep for 12 to 18 hours. 6. Lift out the basket and let it drain. Shorter steeps give a brighter brew; longer steeps give a heavier one. (F5, F8, F9, F10)
## No dedicated jar? Using a French press
   The same method in a French press: steep coarse coffee in the fridge, then press and decant so the coffee stops extracting. The 1 litre capacity means scaling the recipe down to about 100 g of coffee per litre. (F52, F53, F58)
## Choosing beans for cold brew
   Cold extraction mutes acidity and brings out sweetness and chocolate. Medium roasts with caramel and chocolate notes are a reliable choice. Colombia Huila is a strong match, and the 1 kg bag suits regular batches. Fruit-forward light roasts can also be used for a brighter cup. (F20, F22, F11, F14, F15)
## Diluting, serving and storing
   Dilute the concentrate roughly 1:1 with water or milk over ice and adjust to taste. Keep it sealed and cold, and use it within about a week. Covers serving ideas and how to troubleshoot a sour or bitter batch. (F7, F8, F9)
Product cards: P1, P2, P3
Links: P1, P2, P3, L1, L2, L3
</plan>

{"title":"How to Make Cold Brew Coffee at Home: Ratio, Grind and Steep Time","meta_description":"Learn how to make cold brew coffee at home: the coffee-to-water ratio, coarse grind size, steep time, a step-by-step method, bean choice and serving tips.","slug":"how-to-make-cold-brew-coffee-at-home","markdown":"To make cold brew coffee, steep coarsely ground coffee in cold water in the fridge for roughly 12 to 18 hours, then separate the grounds from the liquid [G]. A ratio of about 1:10 coffee to water gives a smooth concentrate that you dilute roughly 1:1 with water or milk before drinking [G]. The rest of this guide covers why that works, what equipment you need, and how to adjust each variable for the cup you want.

## What cold brew is, and why time replaces heat

Cold brew is an immersion method. Instead of passing water through a bed of coffee, as in pour-over, you leave the grounds sitting in the water for the whole brew. Hot water extracts flavour in minutes; cold water does the same job far more slowly, so the brew needs many hours rather than minutes.

That slow, cold extraction changes which compounds end up in the cup. Many of the sharper acids and bitter compounds that hot water pulls out readily are extracted less, so the result tastes rounder, sweeter and lower in bitterness. The trade-off is that some of the bright, aromatic top notes of a hot cup are muted.

Our Cold Brew Jar is an immersion brewer built around this principle, with a recommended steep of 12 to 18 hours in the fridge [F2, F10].

### Cold brew is not iced coffee

The two are often confused. Iced coffee is brewed hot and then cooled, usually by pouring it over ice, so it keeps the acidity and aroma of hot coffee. Cold brew never touches hot water at all. If you want a bright, crisp chilled drink, iced coffee is the route; if you want something smooth and chocolatey that holds up well to milk, cold brew is the better choice.

## What you need

The equipment list is short, but each item affects the result:

- **A vessel with a filter.** You need something to hold the coffee and water together for many hours and a way to remove the grounds cleanly afterwards.
- **A burr grinder that grinds coarse.** Blade grinders produce a mix of dust and chunks; burrs give an even, coarse grind.
- **A scale.** Weighing coffee and water is the only reliable way to repeat a batch you like.
- **Cold, filtered water.** Cold brew is mostly water, so off-flavours from heavily chlorinated or very hard water carry straight through.
- **Fresh beans.** Coffee roasted within the last few weeks and ground just before brewing gives the sweetest result.

The dedicated option in our range is the [Cold Brew Jar](P1), a 1.5 litre glass jar made by Fernhill [F1, F3, F4]. It has a fine stainless steel filter basket that holds the grounds, so there is no separate filtering step, and an airtight lid that keeps fridge odours out while it steeps [F5, F8].

{{P1}}

## Ratio and grind size

### Start at 1:10 for concentrate

A reliable starting point for cold brew concentrate is about 1 part coffee to 10 parts water by weight [G]. In the Cold Brew Jar that works out neatly: the filter basket holds up to 150 g of coarse ground coffee, and the jar makes 1.5 litres of concentrate [F6, F7]. If your batches come out too strong or too weak after dilution, change the ratio in small steps rather than changing the steep time and ratio together, so you know which adjustment made the difference.

### Why the grind must be coarse

Grind size matters more in cold brew than many people expect. Aim for a coarse grind, similar to what you would use for a French press. There are two reasons:

1. **Fines over-extract.** Over a long steep, tiny particles give up their bitter compounds and make the brew taste harsh and drying.
2. **Fines cloud the brew.** Dust-like particles pass through filters and leave a muddy, silty concentrate that keeps extracting in the bottle.

An even, coarse grind lets water reach every particle at a similar rate, which is what produces the clean, sweet profile cold brew is known for.

### Grinding enough coffee

Our [Hand Grinder](P3) has 30 external click settings running from espresso to French press, so its coarse end covers cold brew [F26, F27]. Its 38 mm hardened stainless steel conical burrs are designed for consistent particle size [F25]. The hopper holds 25 g of beans, so a full 150 g batch for the Cold Brew Jar means grinding in several loads [F6, F28]. That is manageable for a weekly batch, and the coarse setting grinds faster than a fine one.

{{P3}}

If you plan to brew large batches often, an electric grinder will save effort; you can compare options in our [grinder collection](L1).

## Step by step: making cold brew in the jar

1. **Weigh and grind.** Weigh up to 150 g of whole beans and grind them coarse [F6].
2. **Fill the filter basket.** Tip the grounds into the fine stainless steel filter basket and set it in the jar [F5].
3. **Add water slowly.** Pour cold, filtered water over the grounds in stages, letting each pour soak in before the next. The aim is to wet every particle; dry pockets of coffee extract unevenly. A gentle stir with a spoon helps break up any clumps.
4. **Seal and refrigerate.** Fit the airtight lid and place the jar in the fridge; it is sized to fit in a fridge door [F8, F9].
5. **Steep.** Leave it for 12 to 18 hours [F10].
6. **Lift out and drain.** Lift out the filter basket and let it drain into the jar before setting it aside [F5]. Avoid squeezing or pressing the grounds, which pushes fines and bitterness into the concentrate.

### Adjusting steep time

Within the recommended window, steep time is your main flavour dial. A shorter steep gives a lighter, brighter concentrate with more of the coffee's fruit character. A longer steep gives a heavier, more chocolatey and fuller-bodied brew. Pick a time, note it down, and move it in steps of a couple of hours until the balance suits you.

## No dedicated jar? Using a French press

A French press works well for cold brew because it is also an immersion brewer with a built-in filter. Our French Press is a 1 litre immersion brewer with a four-layer mesh filter [F52, F53, F58].

Because it holds less than the jar, scale the recipe down. At a 1:10 ratio, a litre of water needs about 100 g of coffee [G]. The method is otherwise the same:

1. Add the coarse grounds to the empty beaker.
2. Pour in cold, filtered water slowly, stir gently to wet all the grounds, and set the plunger on top without pressing.
3. Cover and place in the fridge for the steep.
4. Press the plunger down slowly and steadily.
5. Decant the concentrate straight away into a sealed bottle or jar.

That last step matters. If the coffee stays in the beaker on top of the grounds, it keeps extracting and turns bitter. You can browse more options in our [immersion brewer collection](L3).

## Choosing beans for cold brew

Cold extraction mutes acidity and brings sweetness, body and chocolate notes forward. That makes medium roasts with caramel and chocolate character a dependable choice: their strengths are exactly what cold brew emphasises.

Our [Colombia Huila](P2) is a strong match. It is a washed-process, single-origin coffee roasted to a medium level [F11, F15, F20]. Its tasting notes of red apple, caramel and milk chocolate translate well to a cold steep, where the caramel and chocolate tend to lead [F22]. It comes in 250 g and 1 kg bags, and the larger size suits anyone brewing a jar every week [F14].

{{P2}}

Fruit-forward light roasts are worth trying if you want a brighter, more unusual cold brew. Our Ethiopia Guji, natural process is a light roast with tasting notes of blueberry, dark chocolate and jasmine [F41, F42]. Expect a cup that is less classic but more aromatic, and consider a slightly longer steep to build body. The full selection is in our [coffee beans collection](L2).

## Diluting, serving and storing

### Diluting

The 1.5 litres from the Cold Brew Jar is concentrate, not ready-to-drink coffee [F7]. A good starting point is to dilute it about 1:1 with cold water or milk and pour it over ice [G]. Taste and adjust: some prefer it stronger for drinking with milk, others lighter for drinking black.

### Serving ideas

- **Black over ice:** concentrate and water, plenty of ice.
- **With milk:** concentrate and cold milk or a plant milk; the low acidity means milk is less likely to taste sharp against it.
- **Sparkling:** top the concentrate with sparkling water for a lighter, refreshing drink.
- **Hot:** dilute the concentrate with hot water for a smooth, low-bitterness hot cup.

### Storing

Keep the concentrate sealed and cold. In the Cold Brew Jar, the airtight lid and fridge-door fit make it easy to store the batch where it was brewed [F8, F9]. Use homemade concentrate within about a week, as its flavour gradually flattens and turns stale [G].

### Troubleshooting a batch

| Problem | Likely cause | What to change |
|---|---|---|
| Sour, thin or weak | Under-extraction | Steep longer, grind a little finer, or use more coffee |
| Bitter or harsh | Over-extraction | Steep shorter or grind coarser |
| Muddy or silty | Too many fines | Grind coarser and do not squeeze the grounds |
| Flat or stale | Old beans or old concentrate | Use freshly roasted beans and brew smaller batches more often |

Change one variable at a time and write down what you did. After two or three batches, you will have a recipe you can repeat every week."}
